annotation.reasoning_summary: The dataset maps individual building blocks managed by housing associations. Despite the high number of features, they are distinct real-world assets rather than a partition of space or statistical units. Topology metrics (low shared_boundary_ratio, low convex_hull_fill_ratio) confirm they should be classified as PlainVectorRegion containing objects.
The layer represents discrete archaeological finds and cesspits at specific locations, which are real-world objects/sites, making this an ObjectDS. The geometry consists of points.
The dataset maps specific archaeological find locations (points). Each point represents a discrete, identifiable archaeological object or find site, which fits the ObjectDS definition.

The map features represent discrete, identifiable archaeological sites (real-world objects) rather than reporting units or continuous coverage. The low shared boundary ratio and low convex hull fill ratio confirm these are isolated polygons representing specific locations.

The polygons represent specific selected park areas where barbecue rules apply, rather than a full-area partition or administrative grid. As the areas are bounded patches, it is classified as PatchDS.

The dataset represents specific designated conservation areas (protected city and village views), which are identifiable real-world managed places/assets. As these areas do not cover the entire city but exist as distinct, selected polygons, they are classified as PlainVectorRegion and ObjectDS.

The layer maps point locations where wild bee observations were recorded, treating each location as a distinct site of ecological inventory. The properties are categorical descriptors of the observations at these specific sites rather than continuous spatial measurements or counts, making ObjectDS the most appropriate classification.

The layer maps specific locations of beehives. Each point represents a distinct real-world facility or collection of hives (ObjectDS), even though they possess attributes detailing the number of hives at each location.

The dataset partitions the city into predefined soil quality zones, representing an area-wide thematic classification of soil types; this satisfies the requirements for VectorTessellation and CoverageDS.
The dataset maps individual trees, which are distinct, countable real-world objects. The geometry consists of points, and each point represents a single tree asset managed by the municipality.

The dataset contains individual tree records (points) managed by the city. Each point represents a distinct real-world object (a tree), making it an ObjectDS. Numeric attributes like age or radius are properties of these individual objects rather than the primary mapped phenomenon.

The dataset maps individual trees as points, which are discrete, identifiable real-world objects. While it contains attributes like species and height, it is fundamentally an inventory of assets (trees) and thus falls under ObjectDS.
The dataset maps individual trees as point features, which are distinct, real-world managed assets. This falls under the ObjectDS category.
The layer represents specific neighborhood composting initiatives, which are discrete, identifiable, real-world objects/facilities. Each point is a distinct project with associated attributes.

The layer identifies specific, bounded zones labeled as 'Cameragebieden' (camera areas). Based on the low shared_boundary_ratio and the nature of these zones as isolated patches of surveillance rather than a full-area partition, PlainVectorRegion and PatchDS are the correct classifications.

The dataset maps individual trees (Canadian poplars) as point features. Each point represents a distinct real-world object (a tree) with associated management attributes, classifying it as an ObjectDS.
The layer represents physical sensor locations (telsystemen) used for crowd monitoring. As discrete countable real-world facilities/assets, these are classified as ObjectDS.

The map depicts specific, bounded study areas for cultural-historical research. These do not cover the city exhaustively, nor are they statistical units or objects, making them PatchDS features. The geometry is PlainVectorRegion due to the relatively low shared_boundary_ratio and the specific, selective nature of these study areas.

The dataset maps individual sites/locations of knotweed infestations as points. Each point represents a distinct real-world object (an infestation site) with descriptive attributes, making it an ObjectDS.

The layer maps specific, identifiable ecological bottleneck locations and their associated mitigation solutions (ecopassages) as points. These are discrete, managed assets/facilities, making ObjectDS the most appropriate classification.

The dataset represents isolated potential wind energy areas. These are selected bounded patches of land and do not form a complete coverage (tessellation). Despite numeric attributes like potential capacity, the primary purpose is identifying specific project/development zones, classifying them as PatchDS.

The dataset represents point-based locations (polling stations) where election results are aggregated. Although the points contain extensive numeric vote data, they are fundamentally identified by their function as specific real-world voting facilities, making ObjectDS the most appropriate entity type.

The layer represents discrete, identifiable caterpillar nest locations in trees, which are distinct real-world objects. While it contains attributes like priority and date, these describe the objects rather than mapping numeric quantities or events.

The dataset represents specific geographical areas where pedicab regulations (rules and access zones) apply, which are not exhaustive, thus functioning as a patch map. Low adjacency and topology hints confirm PlainVectorRegion.
The dataset maps pedicab (fietstaxi) and carriage (koets) stands as discrete point facilities, which qualifies them as ObjectDS.

The dataset maps individual address locations (non-residential functions) in Amsterdam as point features. Each point represents a distinct real-world facility or business object, which is best classified as ObjectDS.

The dataset represents a thematic classification of function mixes across the city using block-street polygons. Although the topology indicates a fragmented structure (PlainVectorRegion), the dataset provides an exhaustive thematic coverage of urban function types, making it a CoverageDS.

The dataset represents administrative neighborhood combinations (Buurtcombinaties) that partition the city of Amsterdam. As reporting and statistical units covering the area, they qualify as VectorTessellation for geometry and LatticeDS for entity.
The dataset represents neighborhood divisions (Buurtcombinaties) in Amsterdam which form a complete administrative partition of the study area, qualifying it as VectorTessellation and LatticeDS.

The layer represents official neighborhood boundaries in Amsterdam, which form a complete administrative partition of the city. The high shared boundary ratio and topological indicators confirm it as a VectorTessellation, and it serves as a standard administrative reporting unit (LatticeDS).

The layer represents neighborhood boundaries partitioning the city of Amsterdam. These are administrative units used for reporting and statistical aggregation, clearly fitting the VectorTessellation geometry and LatticeDS entity definition.
The layer represents city districts (stadsdelen) which form a complete administrative partition of Amsterdam. This constitutes a VectorTessellation of reporting units, classified as LatticeDS.

The dataset represents administrative city districts (Stadsdelen) that partition the city of Amsterdam. As they serve as the administrative spatial units for the area, this is classified as a VectorTessellation of LatticeDS reporting units.

The dataset partitions the study area into 25 administrative areas used as reporting units. The high shared boundary ratio and tessellation nature confirm VectorTessellation and LatticeDS.

The dataset represents administrative 'practice areas' in Amsterdam that cover the region. Given the high shared boundary ratio and its nature as a reporting unit for districts, it is classified as a VectorTessellation of LatticeDS units.
The layer represents industrial noise contours expressed in decibel bands (e.g., 50dB), which functions as a contour dataset representing intervals of a continuous phenomenon.

The dataset represents noise level contours (isoline-based interval bands) for air traffic, which are clearly defined by the 'KLASSE' property. Although they share boundaries, they represent interval ranges of a continuous phenomenon rather than administrative or thematic coverage partitions, making ContourDS the most accurate entity type.

The dataset maps noise level intervals (decibel bands) as polygon zones. These are discrete spatial representations of numeric ranges (contours) rather than a complete partitioning of the area or discrete administrative reporting units.

The dataset represents noise contours using polygons that correspond to numeric dB intervals (classes). Although there are many polygons, they represent graduated intervals rather than a complete partition (tessellation), making PlainVectorRegion and ContourDS the most accurate labels.

The dataset maps election results at discrete, named stemlocaties (polling stations), which are facilities/assets. Although they carry extensive numeric results, the primary entity is the polling station itself as a point object.

The map layer represents individual green roofs at specific point locations. Each point is a distinct facility/object with attributes like address, type of garden, and surface area, making it an ObjectDS.

The layer represents land-use categories across the study area. With a high shared_boundary_ratio (0.9385) and nearly full-area coverage, it conforms to the definition of VectorTessellation. As it provides a full-area thematic classification of land use, it is best classified as CoverageDS.
The layer represents archeological findings and historical locations as individual point features, each with specific attributes, qualifying it as an ObjectDS.

The dataset maps selected areas (dog parks, prohibition zones) which are discrete patches rather than a complete administrative partition (tessellation) or coverage. The dataset represents distinct, identifiable green areas (parks, cemeteries, sports parks) within Amsterdam, which are treated as discrete managed objects rather than a complete exhaustive thematic coverage (tessellation). The dataset represents specific individual elm trees (real-world objects) at point locations. Each feature is an identifiable physical asset, making ObjectDS the most appropriate entity type.
The dataset represents specific youth and student housing locations (points) as distinct real-world facilities, which are best classified as ObjectDS.

The dataset maps individual monuments represented by points. Each point corresponds to a distinct real-world asset or location, making ObjectDS the correct entity.

The layer represents discrete cultural heritage sites (monuments) in Amsterdam. Each point corresponds to a specific building or location, fitting the definition of an ObjectDS.

The dataset represents distinct, named parks and public green areas, which are identifiable real-world objects. The low shared boundary ratio and low convex hull fill ratio confirm these are discrete, non-tessellating objects.
